title: The king of the island
hook: tradition places Nanak at the court of Raja Shivnabh in the south, who waited years to meet him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid's successor, and a Sufi's couplets passed on at Pakpattan. Your line was the verses kept. Whose words did you copy down before they were lost? Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

A trader steps off a boat onto an island in the far south, with goods to sell and habits people there notice. On a day when the town keeps a fast, he doesn't. He gets up before dawn, sings, and then goes to work. Word reaches the palace, and the king sends for him. Who taught you to live like this? The trader gives a name, a teacher far away in the north. And the king, the story says, decides he will not rest until that teacher stands in his court. Today: the king of the island.
screen: `A TRADER STEPS OFF A BOAT.` → `WHO TAUGHT YOU TO LIVE LIKE THIS?` → `THE KING DECIDES TO WAIT.`

segments.voice: The janamsakhis call him Raja Shivnabh, a king on an island in the south. The trader is remembered as Bhai Mansukh, a Sikh of Guru Nanak. Tradition says the king asked him how he would know the Guru if he came, and Mansukh said, roughly, you'll know when your heart goes quiet. So the king waited. Not a week. In the telling, years. And waiting made him a target. Word got out that the king longed for a holy man, so pretenders started to arrive, dressed for the part, full of fine speeches, hands out for gifts. The king received every one. None of them was the one. Then, the story goes, a traveler sat down quietly in a garden outside the city, with a companion and a rabab, and began to sing. No announcement. When the king came, he tested him, sending dancers and gifts to see whether this man too could be bought or flattered. Nanak was not moved. And the king's heart, at last, went quiet. What does the story know about waiting? That it was real: Shivnabh didn't settle for the nearest impressive person. That the imitations came first, because a long wait draws them, and part of waiting well is telling the loud thing from the true thing. That the real one arrived plainly, and sat in a garden, not on a throne. And it knows something about the trader. One person living honestly on an island was the whole reason a king started looking.
screen: `A SIKH TRADER ON THE ISLAND.` · `THE KING WAITS, AND IMITATORS COME.` · `A SINGER SITS IN A GARDEN.` · `THE KING'S HEART GOES QUIET.` · then, large: `WORTH THE WAIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait patiently for one thing. Choose something you're waiting on right now. A reply. A result. A person to change. A season of life to end. Name it once, quietly. Then, for the sit, don't reach for the phone and don't rehearse what happens next. Just wait, the way the king waited, with the door open. Notice the urge to grab the nearest substitute, and let it pass. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
The king of the island. Raja Shivnabh, who in the story waited for Nanak, turned away every imitation, and knew the true one when his heart went quiet.
screen: `THE KING OF THE ISLAND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: worth the wait. Today, when something is slow, say the line once instead of settling for the first quick thing on offer. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs retell the sakhi of Raja Shivnabh as a story of longing and recognition, and gurdwaras connected with Guru Nanak's southern journey keep his memory.

notes: Audit pass: hook's 'he keeps no fast days. He bows to no idol' cut, since it made the islanders' worship the foil for the Sikh trader; now only that he didn't keep the town's fast day (the detail the Mansukh sakhi turns on) and rose early to sing and work. Confirm the fast detail against the telling used.
The island is often identified with Sri Lanka (Singhaladip in the janamsakhis); the script says only 'an island in the south'. Confirm whether to name it.
